Payments in Nigeria

Okra

Who would choose to pay by bank when they already had a way to pay?

Role
Manager, Strategy & Product
Period
2021–2024
Focus
Enterprise payments

What would make someone switch?

We were preparing to launch OkraPay, Okra’s payments product, in Nigeria. Our product, design and engineering leads looked to Plaid and Stripe Link for inspiration. From their experience in North America and Europe, a checkout that remembered your details and took a few taps was an appealing starting point.

I kept coming back to the choices I had as a customer in Nigeria. If paying by bank added a step, I could just pay another way. I’d shared that concern and the data behind it in product meetings. We still disagreed about whose problem a new payment option would solve.

The ride from the airport

When our global team came to Nigeria for an offsite, I picked up our head of engineering at the airport. At his hotel, he was ready to get out of the car. He expected his saved card to be charged. I opened my banking app, transferred the fare to the driver, and we waited until the driver confirmed he’d received it.

That wait gave us something concrete to discuss. For the driver, seeing the money arrive was part of finishing the ride. During the offsite, I took the team on more rides and spent time with them watching customers pay merchants. We could now ask which step a bank connection would improve for each person involved.

Choosing who to build for

I proposed that we focus on platforms with a reason to connect a bank account. Consider a creator platform. A customer topping up a balance already has several ways to pay. When the platform pays a creator, it needs to verify the account and send earnings to the right person. A ride platform settling with drivers gave us a second example.

We agreed to prioritize enterprise customers with those kinds of payment needs. That choice gave product, design and engineering a shared way to decide which use cases belonged in the launch.

What happened after launch

I led the go-to-market work that brought OkraPay its first eight adopters in Nigeria. The product went on to process more than $100 million in payments.

That experience changed how I handle a stalled product debate. Now I ask which part of the customer’s day each of us has actually seen. In this case, a few minutes waiting for a driver to confirm a transfer made our next product discussion more useful than the presentation I’d already given.
